title: A Tradition You Have Not Seen

items.prompt: Predict the order of these stages of Bagru hand block printing.

options.label: Mordant printing (chhapai) with syahi and begar
Yellow over-dyeing by sponging (haldi-naspal putai / potai)

config.account:
Bagru hand block printing is a tradition you have not seen. These are its stages, in no particular order.
Mordant printing (chhapai) with syahi and begar: The fabric is printed with two mordants: ferrous syahi from rusted horseshoe nails, and aluminium sulphate begar.
Resist printing with dabu (dabu chhapai): Dabu is applied with a wooden block, sawdust is sprinkled over it, and the fabric is dried in the sun before dipping in indigo.
Washing off excess mordant (khulai): The printed fabric is washed in running water to remove excess mordant before dyeing.
Final washing (dhulai) and finishing: The fabric is left in tanks 3-4 hours until the resist softens, then beaten on a flat stone slab where water flows.
Alum after-mordanting (fitkari rangai): The fabric is dipped for a few minutes in diluted alum, squeezed, dried flat, then stored folded in dark places for at least 3-4 days so the yellow sets.
Yellow over-dyeing by sponging (haldi-naspal putai / potai): Before yellow dyeing, the fabric is again printed with dabu to retain some blue areas.
Scouring (hari sarana / teluni): Scouring, locally 'hari sarana', removes starch, oil and dust; cloth was left overnight in cow dung and water.
Indigo dyeing (neel rangai): The cloth is folded like sari pleats, lowered into the tank, and each pleat opened under the liquid so dye reaches evenly.
Harda treatment (peela karna): Harda powder is mixed with water, the cloth submerged, squeezed and dried flat; then folded and beaten to remove excess harda. This is called peela karna.
Dyeing in alizarin/madder (rangai, bhatti): The dye reacts with two mordants at two locations on the same print, giving red (with alum) and black (with ferrous).
Ageing / drying (sukhai): Printed fabric is left at least three to four days so the mordant paste penetrates the fibre; the longer the ageing, the better the result.

title: A Tradition You Have Not Seen

items.prompt: Which stage comes straight after Sun-drying the resist?

config.account:
Dabu mud-resist block printing is a tradition you have not seen. These are its stages, in no particular order.
Dip-dyeing (usually indigo): The cloth is dip-dyed after the paste hardens.
Dusting the wet resist: Paste areas are immediately covered with sawdust to prevent smudging.
Washing / scouring the cloth: The fabric is first washed to remove impurities that could block dyeing.
Collecting and soaking the mud: Mud is dug from a dry pond and soaked overnight in a separate tank.
Airing and drying: The cloth turns green, then deepens to indigo as it oxidises in air.
Preparing the resist paste: The paste is kneaded by stamping over several days, then strained before use.
Optional pre-printing of colour (naphthol red): Naphthol is printed on areas to be red, sun-dried, then dipped in red salt.
Repeating resist-dye cycles (double/triple dabu): The resist-and-dye sequence is repeated through a dye bath for each colour needed.
Block-printing the resist: Craftsmen dip blocks in the mud, gum and lime paste and press them onto fabric.
Sun-drying the resist: The fabric is sun-dried until the paste hardens.
Washing off the resist: The fabric is washed to remove paste and excess dye.
